description_full: General Motors Company designs, builds, and sells trucks, crossovers, cars, and automobile parts worldwide. It operates through GM North America, GM International, and GM Financial segments. The company markets its vehicles primarily under the Buick, Cadillac, Chevrolet, GMC, Baojun, and Wuling brand names. In addition, it sells trucks, crossovers, cars, and automobile parts through retail dealers, distributors and dealers, as well as to fleet customers, including daily rental car companies, commercial fleet customers, leasing companies, and governments. Further, the company offers various range of after-sale services through dealer network, such as maintenance, light repairs, collision repairs, vehicle accessories, and extended service warranties. Additionally, it provides automotive financing; and software-enabled services and subscriptions. General Motors Company was founded in 1908 and is based in Detroit, Michigan.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 156K people. Revenue per employee of $1.2M ranks in the top quartile among Consumer Cyclical peers. Each employee generates $113K of free cash flow annually. Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (6/10).
financial_summary: General Motors Company is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $71.9B market cap on $185.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 24% against a 10% cost of capital — a 14-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $17.6B in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 9.96× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 0.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 9.3% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 385 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 10% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 9% below the high.

val: The stock trades 69% below its DCF fair value of $274, a meaningful margin of safety.

The 24 covering analysts target $101 on average, 19% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.

ROE of 4% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (4.6x equity multiplier).

hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $27.7B (29% of market cap).
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.21 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.7% over 3 years, 8.6% over 5 years and 2.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 18% of profits supports about 4.4% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 9.1% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a backlog worth 0% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 19%.
Capex runs only 0.8x depreciation (5.0% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 18, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 90%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (29 sales, net $106.2M sold).
It returns 9.3% a year to shareholders (8.4% in buybacks and 0.8% in dividends).
